title: Fluorescence Recovery after Merging a Droplet to Measure the Two-dimensional Diffusion of a Phospholipid Monolayer
protocol: Clean a 4 ml vial with a polytetrafluoroethylene coated cap using acetone.
Clean the same vial using ethanol.
Clean the vial with deionized water.
Blow nitrogen gas thoroughly into the cleaned vial.
Dissolve 1 mg of phospholipid in 1 ml of chloroform to obtain a 1 mg/ml solution.
Add dye tagged phospholipids with less than 1 mol % of the phospholipid solution if visualization is required.
Wrap the vial with polytetrafluoroethylene tape.
Store the sample in a freezer at -20 °C.
Clean a Petri dish (55 mm in diameter and 12 mm in height) with ethanol.
Clean the Petri dish using deionized water.
Fill the Petri dish with 10 ml of deionized water to create an air-water interface.
Spread few microliters of the phospholipid solution onto a clean interface using a micro-syringe.
Wait for at least 30 minutes to evaporate the solvent completely.
Measure the surface pressure of the phospholipid monolayer with a Wilhelmy plate tensiometer.
Wait for at least 30 minutes if filter paper is used as a Wilhelmy plate to get it wetted enough.
Adjust the deposited amount of the phospholipid to control the surface pressure precisely.
Add 4 μl of the DOPC solution (1 mg/ml) onto the 30.25 cm² interface if ~5 mN/m of surface pressure is required.
Use a cone-shaped apparatus with a 3 mm reservoir and two thin channels connected to a large section of the Petri dish to suppress convective flow of the monolayer.
Match water levels between the inside and outside of the cone-shape apparatus.
Place a glass capillary (o.d. 1 mm, i.d. 0.78 mm, length 100 mm) on a capillary holder of a micropipette puller.
Design a program for pulling the capillaries with appropriate parameter values (Heat: Ramp, Pull: 60, Vel: 70, Delay: 70 and Pressure 200).
Pull the capillaries with the designed program according to manufacturer’s protocol.
Absorb phospholipids onto the droplet surface.
Clean a slide glass using acetone, ethanol, and deionized water at least three times.
Place the tapered capillary on a cleaned slide glass, and tilt the capillary to facilitate touching the slide glass with a tip end.
Drop a few droplets of phospholipid solution (1 mg/ml) onto the tip end of a capillary that is adhered to the glass slide using a glass syringe.
Wait at least 30 min to evaporate the solvent completely.
Clean a vial.
Remove water from the vial.
Dry 2 ml of phospholipid solution (1 mg/ml) by applying nitrogen gas gently.
Desiccate the vial for 1 hr at RT in a fume hood to eliminate any remaining solvent.
Add 2 ml of deionized water into the vial containing dried lipids.
Incubate the vial in an oven at 60 °C for 1 hr.
Shake the vial several times.
Sonicate (HF-frequency: Up to 40 kHz, Power: 370 W) for 30 min to obtain vesicles.
Perform extrusion and freeze-thaw processes to obtain monodisperse unilamellar vesicles.
Fill a tapered capillary with 10 µl of deionized water.
Alternatively, fill the capillary with 10 µl of the vesicle solution.
Connect the capillary to an automated micro-injector to provide pressure to form the droplet.
Mount the capillary connected to a micro-injector to a micromanipulator to control the position of the capillary precisely.
Prepare a bright field microscope with a 10X objective lens for imaging the lateral view of the capillary.
Attach a CCD camera to the microscope for visualization.
Position the tip end using a micromanipulator so that it is well visualized under Microscope 1.
Apply variable pressure (~100 hPa) at the tip end of the capillary.
Form an appropriate size droplet (~100 μm in diameter).
Monitor and control the location of the droplet during imaging.
Prepare an inverted microscope set with a 10X objective lens and tube lens of focal length 17 cm.
Enable both fluorescence and bright field modes on the microscope.
Visualize top views of the droplet using the CCD camera in fluorescence mode.
Move the droplet coated with phospholipid to the flat air-water interface along the z-axis, but do not merge it yet.
Use Microscope 1 to visualize the lateral view of the droplet.
Locate the droplet at the center of the top view of the flat monolayer using the micromanipulator.
Visualize the top view of the flat monolayer in bright-field microscope mode.
Move the droplet further toward the flat interface until it merges onto the interface.
Observe a dark circular region surrounded by a white background using fluorescence mode after successful merging.
Record series of fluorescent images according to time after merging the droplet.
Detect a circular region of interest in a series of fluorescent images recorded during a recovery process.
Set the first image of the series as a reference image.
Convolute the reference image with a white circle whose intensity is uniform and slightly smaller than the radius of the dark area in the reference image.
Find the position that indicates the minimum value in the convolution calculation to set as the center of the region of interest.
Determine the radius of the region of interest by convoluting the reference image with a white circle containing the determined center position and uniform intensity over its whole region.
Convolute the reference image with a white circle that has a slightly larger radius (5%–10%) than the initial radius RS.
Calculate the difference in value between this convolution and another calculation using procedure 4.1.2.1.
Increase both RS and RL by one pixel level and repeat the above procedures from RS = RD/2 to RS = 2RD.
Use an iteration containing source codes from procedure 4.1.2.1 to 4.1.2.3 for repetition.
Find the radius of RS that indicates the maximum difference in value using the embedded function named ‘max’.
Set a circle, determined by its center position and radius found in procedure 4.1, as a region of interest.
Calculate the average intensities of the region of interest in a series of fluorescence images according to time.
Convolute each frame with the region of interest and divide it by the area of the region of interest to calculate the average intensity.

Calculate the fractional intensity using f(t) = (F(t) – Fi)/(Fo – Fi), where F(t) is the average intensity in the circle, Fi is the initial intensity in the circle, and Fo is the background intensity.
Fit the fractional intensity profile with the equation provided to obtain the characteristic diffusion time τ.
Calculate the diffusion coefficient D using the relation τ = a2/4D, where a is the radius of the dark area.
